analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and restores the health insurance rules that existed before it.
analysis.headline: The House passed full repeal of the health care law 245-189 on January 19, 2011, but the Senate never voted on it and the bill died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act as if it had never been enacted, along with the health-related parts of the companion reconciliation law, and restore the older laws they replaced. [S2] [S4] That means the taxes that financed the coverage expansion and the insurance rules protecting people with pre-existing conditions would disappear. The House passed it on a party-line vote in the first month of the new Congress; the Senate put it on its calendar and never brought it up. [S6] [S7]
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households would gain from the repeal of the law's taxes, including the Medicare payroll and investment income surcharges on higher earners. Medical device makers, drug makers, and health insurers would be freed of the fees, rebates, and insurance rules the law imposed on them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners and health industry firms

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act effective as of its enactment and restores every provision of law the Act amended or repealed, undoing the law's coverage expansion, insurance rules, and tax provisions in one step.
Repeals the health-related portions of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, including its title I funding provisions, and restores the prior law.
Declares the bill's own budget effects for pay-as-you-go purposes by reference to a Budget Committee statement, providing a procedural vehicle for the repeal to score as it does.

analysis.who_pays: People who gained coverage and protections under the law — particularly those with pre-existing conditions, families receiving the new subsidies, and Medicare beneficiaries whose drug coverage gap was being closed — would lose them. Repealing the law's taxes also removes the revenue that financed the expansion.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with pre-existing conditions and subsidy recipients

drawbacks.text: The repeal is retroactive in effect — it unwinds the Act 'as of its enactment' — so the entire coverage expansion, the protections for people with pre-existing conditions, and the subsidies disappear together rather than being replaced with any alternative in the bill.

Because the bill restores the older laws, it brings back the pre-2010 insurance market rules and eliminates the taxes the law used to finance its benefits, without enacting any replacement funding for those who had gained coverage.

The strongest good-faith argument for repeal was that the law's mandates and taxes raise costs for businesses and high earners and impose federal rules on the insurance market; the bill delivered that full reversal but offered nothing for the people who had newly gained coverage under the law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a clean reversal, not a redesign: it undoes the health law entirely and restores the older rules, with no substitute coverage for people the law had reached. The benefits are concentrated on high-income households and health industry firms — repeal of the law's taxes and rules — while the costs fall on people with pre-existing conditions, subsidy recipients, and others who had gained protections. Weighing those honestly, the costs to ordinary people are large and the gains accrue to a narrow set of interests.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 245-189 on a near party-line vote in January 2011, the Senate placed it on its calendar without ever holding a vote, and it died when that Congress ended. [S6] [S7]

narrative.text: The bill was introduced January 5, 2011 by Rep. Eric Cantor and referred to eight committees, and the Rules Committee quickly reported a rule giving it seven hours of floor debate. [S1] [S6]

Democrats offered a motion to recommit with instructions requiring that the repeal not take effect unless a majority of House members and senators waived their own Federal Employees Health Benefits coverage; it failed 185-245. [S6] [S7]
The House passed the bill on January 19, 2011, 245-189, with 242 of 242 voting Republicans in favor and only 3 of 193 voting Democrats. [S7]
The Senate received the bill on January 25, 2011, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 3; it was never called up for a vote. [S4] [S6]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, everyone who relied on the Affordable Care Act's coverage expansion and insurance protections kept them. Had it passed, high-income households and health industry firms would have been better off through the repeal of its taxes and rules.

for.name: Eric Cantor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the first day of the new Congress, January 5, 2011.

for.name: 242 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously for passage, 242 to 0 among Republicans voting, supplying nearly all of the bill's 245 votes.

for.name: House Rules Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the rule (H. Res. 26) on January 6 that provided for seven hours of debate and brought the bill straight to the House floor within two weeks of introduction.

for.name: 3 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted for final passage, the only Democrats to do so.

against.name: 189 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted against passage, 189 to 3 among Democrats voting.

against.name: Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up after it was placed on the Senate calendar as Calendar No. 3 in late January 2011; no vote ever occurred.

against.name: Rep. Rob Andrews
against.role: Ranking member, Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions requiring that the repeal take effect only if a majority of House members and senators waived their own federal employee health benefits; the motion failed 185-245.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Publicly declared the repeal bill would not be considered in the Senate, and it never received a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost perfectly by party: 242 of 242 voting Republicans supported passage, while only 3 of 193 voting Democrats did. [S7]

industries.note: Repeal would eliminate the Affordable Care Act's Medicare payroll tax surcharge on high earners and its tax on high investment income — revenue that helped finance coverage for lower- and middle-income families. The gain for top earners is the direct loss of the law's funding.

Repeal frees insurers from the law's rules on coverage denial, pricing, and spending requirements, but also ends the individual mandate and subsidies that brought them millions of new paying customers. Their regained freedom to deny or price out people with pre-existing conditions runs against those people's interests.
The law's excise tax on medical devices would be repealed with the rest of the Act, removing an industry-specific levy that helped fund the coverage expansion.

Repeal would undo the law's requirements on drug manufacturers, including mandatory rebates and the phased closure of the Medicare drug coverage gap — obligations that lowered costs for beneficiaries.
